lessons.title: Three famous cases and what they prove
lessons.subtitle: COMPAS, Amazon's experiment and Gender Shades

sections.title: COMPAS: two fairness measures, one fight
sections.content:
COMPAS is a risk-assessment instrument. In parts of the US justice system its score was one input among several. In 2016 ProPublica examined more than 7,000 scores assigned in Broward County, Florida, and compared them with later arrests. The newsroom reported, among other findings, that Black defendants not arrested again in the observation period had been wrongly classified as high risk more often than comparable white defendants. (Source: Angwin et al., ProPublica, 2016)

Northpointe disagreed: within the risk bands, it argued, the scores were similarly calibrated for the two groups. So the fight was about two measures: calibration within a score against error rates between groups. Chouldechova showed that such criteria generally cannot hold at once where base rates differ, unless prediction is perfect. (Source: Chouldechova, A. (2017). Fair prediction with disparate impact. Big Data, 5(2))

What the analysis proves: a difference under ProPublica's error-rate measure. What it does not prove: which data or design choice caused it. No formula decides which measure counts. Answer that question before such a system is used.
sections.keyTakeaway: Two fairness measures stood against each other in the COMPAS fight. A model can be calibrated within risk bands and still show different error rates between groups.

sections.title: Amazon: an experiment that was stopped
sections.content:
Ten years of applications as training material, many from men. What does a model learn from that? In 2018 Reuters reported, citing people familiar with the project, on an internal experimental Amazon system for rating CVs built on such data. One model penalised terms such as "women's" and the names of two women's colleges. (Source: Dastin, J., Reuters, October 2018)

The team removed the identifiable gender signals. Per the report, it could not guarantee the system would not fall back on other, indirect features. Amazon disbanded the project team by early 2017 and told Reuters recruiters had never used the tool to evaluate candidates.

The case documents a development risk. No more, no less. Historical application data can carry earlier selection patterns. Whether a model takes them over depends on target, features, validation and deployment. A hiring decision caused by this tool the report does not establish.
sections.keyTakeaway: Reuters documented an internal experiment with gender-related ranking effects. Amazon said recruiters never used the tool on candidates. Cite the case, say both.

sections.title: Gender Shades: 0.8 percent against 34.7 percent
sections.content:
In 2018 Joy Buolamwini and Timnit Gebru tested commercial systems from IBM, Microsoft and Face++ on how they classified binary gender from facial images. That was gender classification, not identifying a person through facial recognition, and the difference counts. (Source: Buolamwini, J. & Gebru, T. (2018). Gender Shades. Proceedings of Machine Learning Research, 81)

0.8 percent. That is the highest reported error rate for lighter-skinned men. For darker-skinned women the error rates reached 34.7 percent depending on the system. Substantial intersectional performance differences, measured in commercial products.

The authors also examined the demographic mix of two widely used benchmarks and found representation skews there. The obvious conclusion: so the data were to blame. Without access to each system's training data, you cannot derive that these benchmarks or one data distribution caused every vendor's errors.

What holds is the measured performance difference under the study design. Cause, transfer and today's product performance are three separate questions.
sections.keyTakeaway: Gender Shades measured up to 34.7 percent error for darker-skinned women in commercial gender classification, at most 0.8 percent for lighter-skinned men. It proved no training-data cause for any vendor.

quiz.questionText: Which finding did ProPublica report in the COMPAS analysis?

answerOptions.text: The system was technically defective and produced arbitrary results
White defendants were twice as likely as Black defendants to be wrongly classified as high risk
Under ProPublica's error-rate measure, Black defendants without a later arrest were wrongly classified as high risk more often than comparable white defendants
The system was perfectly fair, but the dataset was too small

quiz.explanation: ProPublica reported different error rates. Northpointe held calibration within the risk bands against that. Chouldechova explains why, with differing base rates, you generally cannot have both at once.

quiz.questionText: What is established about Amazon's experimental recruiting tool?

answerOptions.text: The model was deliberately programmed that way
Reuters reported gender-related ranking effects; Amazon said recruiters never used the tool to evaluate candidates
The system could not detect applicants' gender
Applications from women really were weaker

quiz.explanation: Reuters described an internal experiment that penalised terms such as "women's". Amazon said recruiters never used the tool on candidates. What that establishes is a development risk, not a hiring decision.

quiz.questionText: What did Gender Shades find for commercial gender classification?

answerOptions.text: The systems recognised all faces with similar accuracy
Only cheaper systems had bias problems
At almost 12 percent, darker-skinned men had the highest error rate of the four groups studied
The highest error rate for lighter-skinned men was 0.8 percent, and for darker-skinned women it reached 34.7 percent depending on the system

quiz.explanation: Gender Shades tested binary gender classification by IBM, Microsoft and Face++ and measured substantial intersectional performance differences. Person identification was not the subject, and no training-data cause was proved.

lessons.title: Ethics on three levels: technology, company, society
lessons.subtitle: Spread responsibility without diluting it

sections.title: Level 1: technology
sections.content:
On the technical level three things matter. How good the system is, how its errors spread, where its limits sit.

Attribution methods such as SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) or LIME (Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations) estimate, under chosen model, reference and perturbation assumptions, what single input features contribute to an output. They show no causal effect, and no full explanation of the decision process.

A bias audit compares error or selection rates across sensibly bounded groups. Without suitable targets, denominators, samples and uncertainty figures it says nothing. For high-risk AI systems Article 9 governs a risk-management system, Article 10 holds data and data-governance requirements plus, where relevant, an examination of possible bias, and Article 15 covers accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity. Whether they already apply to a system depends on classification, role and application date.

Technical tests can make risks visible. Whether a purpose is lawful or defensible, they do not decide.
sections.keyTakeaway: Attribution, group metrics and stress tests answer different questions. No single metric explains cause, fairness and permissibility.

sections.title: Level 2: the company
sections.content:
"Who signed this off?" If nobody in the company can answer that, this level has failed. Every deployment needs a named purpose, a responsible role, approval criteria and a documented escalation route.

Where the high-risk provisions apply, Article 12 requires a system capable of automatic logging. Under Article 26(6) deployers generally keep the automatically generated logs under their control for at least six months, unless other law sets a different period. What information is actually there depends on the system and the deployer's access.

An internal review body can help. No rule mandates an "ethics board" everywhere, and a body without expertise, decision authority, documented approval and an incident process is decoration. For reports of infringements and protection of reporting persons, Article 87 refers to Directive (EU) 2019/1937; scope and national law still need checking.
sections.keyTakeaway: Logging duty, retention and internal approval are three separate requirements. Application depends on category, role and date.

sections.title: Level 3: society
sections.content:
What may a system be used for at all? Not a department, not a vendor. Society decides, through laws, rights and routes of control. The AI Regulation, data protection, equal treatment and fundamental rights can apply in parallel and answer different questions.

Article 22(1) GDPR concerns decisions based solely on automated processing, including profiling, that produce legal effects or similarly significantly affect a person. Article 22(2) holds exceptions. For the cases under paragraph 2(a) and (c), paragraph 3 requires at least human intervention, a chance to express a point of view and to contest. For relevant automated decision-making, Articles 13, 14 and 15 hold information duties and access rights on the logic involved, the significance and the envisaged consequences. A claim to source code, or an explanation for every algorithm, it is not.

Does a significant decision hit you? Then check four points separately: was it solely automated? What effect did it have? Does an exception apply? Which information and protection rights apply?
sections.keyTakeaway: Article 22 GDPR concerns solely automated decisions with legal or similarly significant effect, and it has exceptions. Safeguards and information rights you check under Articles 13 to 15 and Article 22.

quiz.questionText: Which retention duty can Article 26(6) place on deployers of high-risk AI systems?

answerOptions.text: Sending a monthly report to the EU AI Office
Generally keeping the automatically generated logs under their control for at least six months, subject to other law
Making every algorithm publicly accessible
Setting up an internal ethics board

quiz.explanation: Where the provisions apply, Article 12 requires the technical capability for automatic logging. Article 26(6) requires the deployer to keep those logs for at least six months, unless other law sets a different period.

quiz.questionText: Which statement about Article 22 GDPR is correct?

answerOptions.text: It creates a right to demand deletion of all your data
Article 22 bans every use of an algorithm in a decision
Article 22 grants an automatic right to see the source code behind any AI output
Article 22 protects against solely automated decisions with legal or similarly significant effect; exceptions and the safeguards required in each case have to be checked

quiz.explanation: Article 22(1) concerns decisions based solely on automated processing with legal or similarly significant effect. Paragraph 2 holds exceptions. Where a contract requires it or the person explicitly consented, paragraph 3 requires at least human intervention, a chance to express a point of view and to contest. Further information rights sit in Articles 13 to 15.

quiz.questionText: What separates the technical level of AI ethics from the societal one?

answerOptions.text: Societal measures are useless because technology moves faster than policy
Technical measures alone already fix what an AI system may be used for
The technical level has clear answers, the societal level has none
Technology can measure and reduce bias but cannot decide which purposes AI may serve; that is a social and political decision

quiz.explanation: Explainability, bias measurement, stress testing: all necessary, none of it answers a political question. A technically optimised facial recognition system can still be pointed at mass surveillance. Whether that is allowed, society decides.

lessons.title: Three checks for real AI deployments
lessons.subtitle: Data, responsibility, oversight route

sections.title: Check 1: separate data from target
sections.content:
"The data were bad." The sentence explains everything and therefore nothing. Historical data can hold earlier inequalities, measurement errors or selection decisions. It does not follow that every model trained on them reproduces the same distortion. Sample, labels, features, target, optimisation, thresholds and deployment all have a say.

So do not just ask where the data came from. Who is represented? What counts as the right result? Which errors are measured for which groups? Was performance tested in the real deployment context?

COMPAS, Amazon and Gender Shades show three different problems. Boil them down to "bad training data" and you have understood none of them.
sections.keyTakeaway: Data origin, target, error metric and deployment context you check separately. Historical data can hold distortions. They do not determine the result.

sections.title: Check 2: map role to duty
sections.content:
"The AI decided." That sentence names no organisation and no legal basis. It names nobody. The AI Regulation does the opposite and assigns duties by actual role and conduct: Article 16 to providers, Article 22 to authorised representatives, Article 23 to importers, Article 24 to distributors, Article 26 to deployers. Article 25 governs the cases in which another operator counts as the provider.

This allocation says nothing blanket about liability, nor about who caused a specific discriminatory outcome. Data protection, equal treatment, employment or civil law can apply on top.

For the individual case, pin down four answers. Who provides the system? Who sets purpose and deployment? Who makes or confirms the decision? Which provision attaches to exactly that conduct?
sections.keyTakeaway: Actual role first, specific duty second. Article 16 and Articles 22 to 26 govern different operators. No blanket sole responsibility follows.

sections.title: Check 3: an oversight route others can walk
sections.content:
Guesses are cheap. An oversight route another person can walk step by step is work. For checkable cases, a fixed process:

1. Document purpose, responsible role, data source and the human decision point.
2. For a significant automated decision, check whether it was solely automated, its effect, which exception might apply and which information or protection rights exist.
3. For suspected synthetic media, preserve the original source and check provenance and context with the Block 2 process.
4. Record finding, uncertainty and the next responsible route separately.

Want an independent read? AlgorithmWatch (algorithmwatch.org), the Algorithmic Justice League (ajl.org) founded by Joy Buolamwini, and netzpolitik.org publish investigations into algorithmic systems, bias and digital regulation.
sections.keyTakeaway: A defensible oversight route documents purpose, role, data, decision, finding and uncertainty. It swaps guesses for checkable steps.

quiz.questionText: Which statement describes the relation between training data and model effect precisely?

answerOptions.text: Because AI developers deliberately want to build discriminatory models
Because models always use too little training data, whatever its composition
Because individual developers unknowingly program their personal preferences into the model
Historical data can hold inequalities; the model effect also depends on target, features, testing and deployment

quiz.explanation: Historical data can mirror earlier inequalities. Whether that becomes a harmful model effect depends further on selection, labels, target, modelling, thresholds, evaluation and deployment.

quiz.questionText: How does the AI Regulation allocate duties along the value chain?

answerOptions.text: Only the original AI developer
Nobody, because AI systems act on their own
Only the market surveillance authority of the relevant EU Member State

By actual role: providers under Article 16, authorised representatives under Article 22, importers under Article 23, distributors under Article 24 and deployers under Article 26; Article 25 governs role changes

quiz.explanation: The duties sit in different articles and attach to the actual role. Article 25 can turn another operator into the provider. Liability, data protection and equal treatment you check separately.

quiz.questionText: Which organisation founded by Joy Buolamwini researches algorithmic bias?

answerOptions.text: AlgorithmWatch
netzpolitik.org
Data & Society Research Institute
Algorithmic Justice League (ajl.org)

quiz.explanation: Joy Buolamwini founded the Algorithmic Justice League (ajl.org). It researches harms and inequities in algorithmic systems and teaches. AlgorithmWatch (algorithmwatch.org) examines algorithmic decision systems in Europe.
